The distribution of wide binary stars in the galaxy's outskirts offers a unique opportunity to test the gravitational laws at low acceleration levels found in the outskirts of galaxies. To do this, we created a sophisticated simulation of wide binaries, taking into account the effects of gravitational interactions with passing stars. Our model, which uses high-precision data from the Gaia mission, allows us to accurately predict the impact of gravitational encounters on the stars' separation over time. Our results show that the predicted distribution of these stars matches the observed data, providing a baseline for further study. To do this, we developed a complex model that considers the effects of gravitational interactions on the stars' separation and velocity, and compared it to the observed data. Our model, which is based on the observed data, allows us to accurately predict the distribution of these stars, and provides a new tool for testing the gravitational laws at low acceleration levels.

To each multiplicative linear logic proof structure, we associate a system of polynomial equations over integers, with connections to logic and algebra. We demonstrate how to apply Gr\"obner bases, a concept from elimination theory, to resolve this system and provide a proof checker for the multiplicative fragment of linear logic.

This paper presents a novel financial time series analysis method that's based on a visual representation called cross-recurrence plots. This method's core idea is to apply a non-linear, synchronized analysis to pairs of time series data, allowing for the detection of complex relationships between market indicators. To measure the relationships between time series states, we employed a combination of distance-based measures and entropy. This approach enables the comparison of cross-recurrence quantification analysis, cross-recurrence entropy analysis, and a new cross-recurrence dimorphism analysis method. This paper's cross-recurrence dimorphism analysis method demonstrates superior performance in detecting time series relationships compared to traditional methods, as shown through the analysis of the volatility and trading volume relationships in the S&P 500 index.

THz radiation's interaction with solid materials is a topic of intense study, but
the specific electronic responses to this interaction are not yet fully
understood. In this research, a theoretical model is developed to investigate
the behavior of a 2D electron gas when subjected to THz radiation, taking into
consideration the unique inertial properties resulting from the circular motion
of particles. The results of this theoretical model are then compared to the
findings of time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy experiments, revealing
distinct patterns of electronic responses that vary based on the polarization
of the incident THz waves.

This study introduces an innovative approach to enhancing click-through rate (CTR) prediction models for online advertising, specifically addressing the challenge of cold-start ads with limited interaction data. A new framework, the Adaptive Ad Ranking system, dynamically adjusts the importance of training data based on ad exposure and user interactions, allowing it to leverage experiences with similar, "warm" ads to improve predictions for "cold" ads. By selectively focusing on the most valuable user-ad interactions, our method significantly outperforms existing techniques, achieving a 10% improvement in AUC over a standard uniform training approach for ads with limited data, while maintaining comparable results for ads with sufficient data. Our approach has been successfully implemented in production and demonstrates substantial practical benefits.

Organizations with extensive business operations frequently encounter complex workflows that are too intricate to be considered structured. To effectively model these intricate processes, additional information is required, such as input data, but existing structured process models lack this necessary detail. This study aims to address this issue by developing a new approach to enrich structured process models with the necessary information to accurately represent complex workflows. The proposed method involves utilizing data from process execution logs to identify and model knowledge-intensive business processes. The results demonstrate that enriching structured process models with data-driven insights can significantly improve their accuracy and effectiveness in representing complex business operations.

Wildfires are increasingly frequent and have a major impact on the atmosphere, which can also be influenced by the atmospheric particles they produce. These particles can significantly reduce solar energy output, which is crucial for solar power generation. This study examines the effect of 2021 California wildfires on solar energy production, which was monitored using solar radiometers and satellite data. These particles caused a notable drop in solar radiation, leading to a temporary decrease in solar power output, which was observed in the region. This decrease was comparable to the drop in solar radiation observed during the 2019 Australian bushfires. These findings highlight the need to consider the impact of atmospheric particles on solar power generation, which is essential for the long-term success of solar energy production.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are disclosed in a short timeframe. To address this issue, we introduce a new location privacy framework that takes into account the interconnections between consecutive locations. Our framework is based on the concept of consecutive locations' indistinguishability, which ensures that disclosed locations remain ambiguous even when they are revealed in sequence. We develop a discrete-time Markov chain model to represent the interconnections between locations and propose an algorithm to calculate the probability distribution of consecutive locations, which is then used to calculate the entropy of the probability distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical examples and show that it outperforms existing privacy protection methods.

The analysis of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data is gaining traction in neuroscience, but a key issue arises when analyzing datasets from multiple sites.  Current research has highlighted the detrimental impact of multisite studies on detecting differences between groups in the frequency of low-frequency oscillations and identifying individual patterns of brain activity.  However, the effect of multisite data on identifying structural changes and using independent component analysis remains unclear.  To address this knowledge gap, a comprehensive simulation study was conducted to evaluate the performance of various statistical methods in analyzing multisite resting-state fMRI data.  The results indicate that multisite data significantly reduces the power of statistical tests that compare the sizes of specific brain regions between two groups.  Moreover, these studies also show a notable decline in the accuracy of identifying independent components using ICA.  In contrast, the use of statistical tests that control the false discovery rate and machine learning methods for pattern recognition was found to be relatively resilient to multisite data.  These findings have important implications for the design of future resting-state fMRI studies and the development of analysis techniques that can effectively handle data from multiple sites.

Building on previous work, we have developed a new definition of Ricci curvature specifically for directed graphs, along with an equivalent characterization in terms of optimal transport. This definition enables us to define directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature, which in turn allows us to establish lower bounds for their Riemannian dilation rate and upper Riesz bound.

Sanskrit-Hindi, a mixed language combining Sanskrit and Hindi, is widely used across South Asia. This particular language blend poses difficulties in creating a unified, standardized written form, which in turn makes it challenging to develop accurate word embeddings. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a new, unsupervised method for creating word embeddings for Sanskrit-Hindi by utilizing a neural network-based word segmentation approach. This innovative technique enables the creation of word embeddings for mixed languages without the need for extensive training data. To validate our approach, we have created a test dataset and compared the generated embeddings with existing methods, including those based on character-level and pre-tokenized word forms. The results indicate that our method outperforms the other approaches in accurately representing segmentable mixed language words.

To understand the behavior of the H$_3$S system, we've developed a theoretical model that takes into account the pressure-dependent density of states near the Fermi level. Our model shows that the critical temperature of the H$_3$S system initially rises with pressure, peaks at around 160 GPa, and then falls off. This theoretical prediction aligns with the experimentally observed $T_c$ values for H$_3$S at lower pressures, and we've also used our model to estimate the $T_c$ values for the hydrides of sulfur at ambient pressure, which can be verified through future experiments.

GWAS studies have uncovered numerous genetic factors associated with various traits and diseases. However, the majority of these findings only demonstrate correlations, not causations. Understanding the causal relationships between genetic variants and phenotypes is essential for developing effective prevention and treatment strategies. This study proposes a novel framework that integrates observational data and prior biological knowledge to identify and prioritize potential causal genetic variants. The proposed approach, called CausalGWAS, employs a stepwise method to establish a connection between phenotypes and genetic factors through intermediary variables. When applied to two large-scale studies, CausalGWAS outperformed existing methods in predicting phenotypes and demonstrated the ability to reveal meaningful biological relationships.

This paper introduces a novel control system for advanced bipedal robots, which incorporates both powerful thrusters and weaker friction forces to achieve dynamic walking. We develop a simplified, yet accurate, mathematical model that describes a robot's movement during the leg swing phase, which is based on real-world conditions. To maintain stable walking, we create a control system that uses real-time data to calculate the necessary adjustments in thrust and leg movement. Our approach is successfully demonstrated through simulations of a realistic bipedal robot, which shows that the thrusters can effectively enable a variety of walking patterns, including changes in speed and direction.

This research introduces a visual relocalization technique that utilizes 3D surfel maps for accurate pose estimation. We present an efficient method to generate these surfel maps by converting existing depth data, which can be produced by devices like the Microsoft Kinect, into a sparse point cloud representation. We then utilize a combination of plane segmentation and the region growing algorithm to identify and create surfels. To achieve reliable relocalization, we employ the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm to estimate pose based on corresponding re-detected and stored surfels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through successful relocalization tests in an indoor environment.

In federated learning, data holders collaborate on training a shared model without sharing their data. However, most current approaches require all participating clients to have fully labeled data, a condition that is often impractical due to the expense of labeling data. This limitation is particularly problematic for clients who have partially labeled data, as they would need to either manually label more data or exclude their data from the training process. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that enables clients with incomplete labels to actively contribute to the federated learning process by generating pseudo labels for unlabeled data based on their local training data and model updates. These clients then share the enhanced data with the central server, which aggregates the model using traditional federated averaging. This approach effectively mitigates the data skew issue and ensures that the model remains robust and representative of the diverse data sources. To further enhance the model's performance, we introduce two additional techniques: one that limits the model's capacity to prevent overfitting, and another that limits the influence of each client to prevent dominant clients from controlling the training process. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving accurate and representative model training.

Following a black hole-neutron star merger, a massive accretion disk forms, leading to a black hole's spin-down via gravitational waves and neutrino radiation, as well as a jet's launch powered by the Blandford-Znajek and magnetorotational processes. Our 3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations reveal that a remnant neutron star's tidal disruption results in a massive accretion disk, whose evolution is characterized by a series of magnetorotational outbursts. These outbursts are triggered by the growth of the $m=2$ and $m=3$ $r$-modes, which are damped by magnetic braking, causing the accretion disk to expand and the black hole's spin to decrease. As a result, the black hole's spin-down leads to a decrease in gravitational wave frequency, whose evolution is consistent with that of a spinning black hole, whose rotation rate is controlled by the accretion disk's evolution.

We demonstrate that the Kawazumi-Zhang invariant of a compact Riemann surface with one hole, denoted as $\Sigma_{1,1}$, can be expressed as a combination of instanton homology groups of its double branched cover over the 2-sphere, denoted as $X_{2,2}$. This expression is initially formulated in terms of instanton homology, and then translated into a topological quantum field theory (TQFT) using the割拼 (cut and paste) principle.

We provide detailed proofs for the existence and uniqueness of the process's quasi-stationary distribution and the conditional semi-group's strong compactness in a polynomially positive Markov process taking values in a Polish space with a decreasing error structure. This result is achieved by establishing a bounded integral equation and proving its strong compactness using a novel approach that combines a mean value theorem and a fixed-point theorem.

In an optical setup where two dielectric particles are aligned along the axis of a graphene sheet, the presence of graphene significantly impacts their optical interaction. The alignment causes the particles to induce surface plasmons in the graphene sheet, resulting in a complex optical force that positions the particles differently compared to a scenario without graphene. The optical force arises from a combination of the particles' dielectric properties and the graphene's properties, allowing for precise control over their position by adjusting the graphene's electrical conductivity. The research also explores the possibility of using this phenomenon to study the properties of the graphene sheet by analyzing the particles' optical behavior.

In the Emergency Department, doctors often have to make quick decisions about which patients to treat first, as they can't give equal attention to all patients at once. This situation creates a complex problem of balancing the needs of multiple patients, which can be modeled as a type of queue management issue. To handle this, we developed a decision-making framework that takes into account how longer treatment times in the ED might affect a patient's admission rates and future health. This framework is based on a well-known mathematical model, which we adapted to deal with an ever-changing group of patients. Our analysis shows that, under certain conditions, extending treatment times can actually reduce admission rates and lead to better patient outcomes.

In multi-agent systems, it is crucial to have a stable state where each agent's strategy remains optimal given the strategies of others, known as Nash equilibrium. This paper focuses on a specific type of equilibrium in which every agent successfully completes its designated task, and we investigate the conditions under which this occurs. We develop an algorithm that allows agents to reach this stable state through distributed computation, and we demonstrate its stability and convergence through a theoretical example.

In heavy-ion collisions, the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) has been investigated through its connection to charge-dependent correlations.  Our research uses simulated Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV to examine the CME-like correlations without the influence of background effects.  The simulation incorporates a hybrid model combining the AMPT and hydrodynamic approaches, which account for the initial collision dynamics and final particle production.  The results show that the hydrodynamic part of the simulation does not generate significant CME-like correlations, but rather produces background-like correlations.  The CME-like correlations arise primarily from the interaction between the charge-to-charge asymmetry of particles and their elliptical flow.  The study reveals that the CME-like signal is sensitive to the charge-to-odd-baryon ratio, which can be used to differentiate the CME signal from background effects in future experiments.

The phenomenon of online crowdfunding has become a significant force in financing, and the analysis of crowdfunding data offers valuable insights into the behavior of contributors. In the context of online crowdfunding, project creators can observe contributors' actions, which serve as behavioral indicators that can influence project funding success. This study aims to uncover the hidden patterns of contributors' behavior in the context of Chinese crowdfunding data, which has not been previously explored. By applying a sophisticated model, we successfully predicted funded projects, and the results showed that the inclusion of funders' behavior significantly improved the accuracy of the prediction, surpassing other traditional methods.

Developing machine learning models to identify network threats using data from diverse sources is a complex task. The process involves integrating data from multiple endpoints, each with its own data collection and labeling procedures, resulting in varied data characteristics. This study presents a novel approach to create a machine learning-based detector that can effectively utilize data from multiple sources. The method employs a weighted aggregation technique to combine data from different sources, allowing the model to adapt to the specific characteristics of each source. The results show that this approach significantly improves detection accuracy when using data from multiple sources, outperforming models trained on individual sources alone.

This study focuses on solving a planning problem for robots, where the objective is to minimize the completion time of an ordered sequence of tasks. The tasks are spatially distributed, and the robot can only move between them, with each task requiring a specific amount of time to accomplish. The optimization problem is formulated as a discrete nonlinear problem, which can be solved efficiently using a proposed algorithm. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through numerical experiments, which demonstrate its effectiveness in producing optimal solutions within a limited time frame.

We have developed an advanced MoSe$_2$/SiN interface, combining high electron mobility with exceptional interface quality. By utilizing Si$_3$N$_8$ as a buffer layer, we achieved a high interface electron mobility of 10,000 cm$^2$/Vs and a low electron trap density of 10$^{10}$ cm$^{-2}$. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the formation of a MoSe$_2$ channel with precise gate control, exhibiting high coherence times in MoSe$_2$ spin qubits. These findings provide a solid foundation for the development of high-performance MoSe$_2$ qubits.

We investigate synchronized patterns in a network of synchronized oscillators with different properties, where different groups of similar oscillators synchronize on distinct timelines. Given the complex nature of these synchronized timelines, we focus on understanding their characteristics. In this research, we focus on zero-timed differences between synchronized timelines of different groups, which are zero-timed differences that remain unchanged regardless of individual timeline shifts. We develop a model to predict these values and test it using a variety of oscillator models, including simple constant values, stable equilibrium points, and chaotic systems.

This study investigates the effect of query language on video search result diversity in major Western search engines. We gathered data from Google, YouTube, and Bing by running 1000 English and 1000 Spanish search queries, and then analyzed the diversity of the results using a new metric called MSHG. We found that a significant portion of the video search results were identical across both languages, and that the majority of the videos came from just a few content creators. We also discovered that a substantial percentage of the videos were from the US, and that a large number of them were educational in nature. Our results indicate that the language of the query has a substantial impact on the diversity of the video search results, and that there is a need for more diverse content creators to be supported.

To expand upon the analytical bootstrap's capabilities, we've developed a technique to analyze supersymmetric monodromy defects in three-dimensional space. Specifically, we've applied this technique to the Wess-Zumino model with a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ monodromy, resulting in a precise determination of the defect's interaction strength and a partial set of additional correlation functions.

We demonstrate that there is exactly one elliptic curve, up to isomorphism, defined over a cubic Galois field extension of rational numbers that includes a point on the curve representing 1/13 of its full cycle. The national field of this special field extension features a prime number as one of its components. We also provide the precise national equation for this unique curve.

The performance of large-scale wireless networks is heavily influenced by interference, which is often disregarded in previous studies. We investigate the impact of interference correlation on user equipment (UE) latency in a large network with correlated interference. We consider a network with numerous base stations and analyze the average latency experienced by UEs. We find that interference correlation significantly impacts latency, resulting in a non-monotonic relationship with the density of base stations. We also find that the latency trends in correlated and non-correlated (independent) interference scenarios can be opposite. We develop a mathematical model to predict the average latency in a network with correlated interference, which is verified through simulations.

The effectiveness of self-supervised learning using pseudo-labels has been widely recognized in recent years, particularly in the domain of graph neural networks. However, existing methods face a significant challenge: pseudo-label errors tend to accumulate and worsen performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel pseudo-labeling framework that selectively minimizes the impact of uninformative samples. By incorporating a pseudo-label confidence threshold and a graph-based label propagation technique, our method only utilizes high-quality pseudo-labels to enhance performance. Experimental results on scarce labeled datasets demonstrate the substantial improvement of our framework over state-of-the-art models.

Recent breakthroughs in vision transformers have propelled them to the forefront of video recognition research. However, current approaches typically rely on pre-processing techniques to generate pixel-level features, which are then fed into a transformer architecture. This often results in a significant loss of temporal-spatial information and a substantial increase in computational costs. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel approach called PatchFormer, which directly learns features at the patch level, thereby preserving the original video structure and reducing the computational burden. Furthermore, we develop a new encoding method called PPE, which effectively captures long-range dependencies and enhances performance. Our experiments demonstrate that PatchFormer outperforms existing pixel- and patch-encoder approaches by a significant margin, achieving a remarkable 2.4% improvement in Top-1 accuracy on the Kinetics-407 dataset.

We examine the one-dimensional asymmetric simple exclusion process with speeds $+\alpha$ and $-\beta$ on a torus of size $2L$, where particles cannot occupy the same spot. As the torus becomes increasingly large, with $L$ approaching infinity, we analyze this process and find that it exhibits certain symmetries. This research is an extension of previously studied cases with uniform particle movement, and the results are based on a paper by Bertini, Cancrini, and Giardinà.

This paper explores a novel approach to wireless communication where power from wireless signals is harnessed to support mobile data networks. By utilizing this technology, we aim to reduce the need for additional infrastructure in a network with multiple base stations. To achieve this, we examine a scenario with multiple users, each having multiple antennas, that can draw power from nearby wireless signals and an external source. We focus on optimizing a network's data transmission capacity by jointly adjusting the power gathering settings and communication signals. Our research reveals that an efficient solution can be found through an iterative process, which we demonstrate converges to a stable outcome. Furthermore, to further enhance this capacity, we develop a method to allocate resources by determining the optimal transmission rates and power usage among the base stations. Our proposed approach is shown to converge to a stable state through an iterative process. Finally, we validate our findings through numerical analysis, which also highlights the potential of our wireless power technology to significantly boost the network's data transmission capacity.

We studied the behavior of weakly interacting Fermi gases in two dimensions, with particles having multiple possible states, by examining the gas's density response to a sudden change in its external constraints. This investigation focused on the BCS-BEC crossover phenomenon, with our findings showing that the response behaves differently in two and three dimensions. In contrast to previous research, our results indicate that the response in two dimensions exhibits a distinct non-universal behavior, with particles becoming more tightly bound as their interaction strength increases.

In the context of microwave optomechanics, an RLC circuit is commonly used to interact with an electromagnetic field and a mechanical oscillator, where the latter typically manifests as a microscopic object like a drum or resonator. Our study reveals that an parallel RLC circuit's inertia and dissipation can be effectively represented by a series RLC circuit with the electromagnetic susceptibility having both even and odd symmetry properties. This finding enables the establishment of optomechanical coupling in a capacitive system comprising a capacitor, an electromagnetic port, and a dielectric particle, thereby facilitating the interaction between the electromagnetic field and a mechanical oscillator.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, with parameters within a specific range. The study also compares recurrence coefficients with those of classical orthogonal polynomials of Askey.

We examine a model of active matter consisting of basic agents that move randomly in a confined space, exhibiting unpredictable navigation patterns near surfaces, which can be likened to a directed exploration strategy. This model, operating in both two and three dimensions, doesn't require complex internal workings or sensory capabilities. As the closeness of an obstacle is detected, the model switches to a slower, more persistent movement, resulting in navigation patterns near walls and ceilings reminiscent of a mix of exploration and localised analysis. This behavior arises from simple physical principles, which we demonstrate through mathematical analysis and simulations in both real and virtual environments.

We've developed a method to quantify chiral characteristics of a 2D spacetime using a modified version of the Cherenkov angle, adapting it for use in a quantum field theory context within a cohomological framework. This adaptation is demonstrated through application to a 2D charged black hole scenario.

To enhance visibility in laparoscopic surgery, a method to eliminate smoke from camera view is essential due to its impact on surgical visibility. We introduce an innovative approach that removes smoke from laparoscopic images by analyzing a single 2D image, which is particularly beneficial as most surgeries utilize a single-camera setup. Our method leverages a pre-processed image to identify the background and a real-time Laplace-sharpening algorithm to clarify the foreground. We tested this approach on 12 real surgery videos, yielding promising outcomes.

We've developed a technique for creating robust quantum gates that's not 
sensitive to variations in pulse frequency when working with trapped ions. 
This technique is based on the Rabi-isolation principle and can be applied 
to multi-qubit operations by using specific frequency ranges for different 
qubits. 
We've taken into account the effects of spectral leakage from two essential 
frequencies and the influence of the laser's finite width. 
We've also developed a method for creating robust gates that's not affected 
by variations in pulse frequency and can be easily implemented experimentally. 
These gates can be used for both single and double quantum bit operations 
and their reliability can be further enhanced by using specific 
characteristics of Bessel-C-Gauss pulses.

Using ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, we investigated the behavior of barium titanate, $\text{BaTiO}_3$, in its paraelectric phase. Our research reveals that modeling this compound using a body-centered cubic structure yields more accurate results than a simple cubic structure. This finding is significant for other perovskite compounds as well. We found that the body-centered structure can be represented by a tetrahedral framework consisting of a central titanium ion surrounded by five oxygen ions, all enclosed within a barium ion shell. This model is in line with recent experimental data obtained through X-ray scattering and supports the idea that the tetrahedral structure is a more versatile and precise description of perovskites, as opposed to the traditional octahedral model.

Multivariate data with a functional component can be effectively analyzed using graphical models, but functional data often come in continuous forms, making traditional methods inapplicable. We propose a new approach to model the relationships between functional data and scalar outcomes, demonstrated through the analysis of retinal scan images and cerebral spinal fluid measurements.

Current quantum processors face limitations due to errors, necessitating the use of quantum error correction which significantly extends the time required for computations. To address this issue, our research presents an error-tolerant, flexible quantum simulator that can handle interactions between multiple qubits and insert arbitrary numbers of ideal or noisy identity gates. By enabling the comparison of circuit outputs with and without noise, our tool facilitates the determination of error correction thresholds for complex quantum algorithms, thus making it possible to evaluate the efficacy of quantum error correction without the need for extensive computations on actual quantum processors.

We examine a specific class of non-convex optimization problems that can be represented as a quadratic form subject to a non-convex constraint. By analyzing these problems through the lens of random matrices, it is possible to determine the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the involved matrices. Our analysis reveals that the concentration of eigenvalues near the boundary of the expected spectral distribution significantly influences optimization complexity. This insight allows us to derive lower bounds on the number of iterations required for gradient-based optimization methods, which in turn provides explicit formulas for optimization complexity. These findings are substantiated by numerical experiments.

Our research reveals that when layers of a specific material are stacked, unique states emerge where two excitation particles from different layers combine to form a distinct energy state with a measurable energy level. This energy level is significantly higher than when a single, isolated layer forms a similar state. We found that the probability of forming this distinct energy state is influenced by the number of layers in the material and the energy required to separate the stacked layers.

This research introduces an innovative method for indoor positioning that leverages the precision of millimeter-wave (mmWave) channel data to accurately pinpoint the location of mobile devices. The proposed approach, called Channel Fingerprinting with Multipath Component Utilization (CFMU), incorporates both direct line-of-sight and reflective signals to create a comprehensive fingerprint that matches live channel data with pre-collected data to determine location. The success of CFMU in utilizing these reflective signals is demonstrated through successful tests in a complex environment, resulting in a highly accurate indoor positioning system with 90 cm average error. The CFMU method is also adaptable to scenarios where some reflective signals are weak or blocked, and can be applied to different frequencies and environments.

Researchers have examined the pair production of specific bosons in high-energy proton-proton collisions, utilizing data collected by the ATLAS experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The analysis, based on 139 fb^-1 of data collected at 13 TeV, focused on events containing two specifically polarized bosons, along with significant transverse momentum and missing transverse energy. The findings showed agreement with theoretical predictions, and established limits on the pair production of specific particles, including vectors, at a confidence level of 95%.

We suggest that the Cotton tensor can serve as the foundation for modifying the Relativity General framework by introducing non-gravitational effects, with the additional Einstein and Weyl tensors representing these effects as phenomenological forces in Newton's second law. Furthermore, it is possible to derive a form of the first law of thermodynamics for horizons in modified Relativity General, with the non-gravitational work term corresponding to a pressure exerted by the extra force. This form can be applied to various types of horizons, including cosmological horizons in de Sitter space, leading to a relationship between dark energy density and the scale factor.

This discussion introduces a generalization of topological spaces known as orthomodular spaces, which are constructed from order-theoretic foundations by utilizing orthomodular frames. We establish a dual relationship between orthomodular spaces and orthomodular frames, which in turn can be seen as a broader concept of topological spaces. Furthermore, we examine the connections between orthomodular spaces, ortholattice valued spaces, and closed subspaces of orthomodular spaces derived from ortholattice valued spaces.

This research proposes an innovative approach to displaying Coq proof scripts as animated sequences, aimed at enhancing comprehension and facilitating modifications. The method has significant implications for both teaching and publishing, with additional benefits including the clarification of minor adjustments and the presentation of multiple, parallel proof arguments.

We derive a Riemann Hypothesis equivalent formula that depends on the fourth power mean of holomorphic cusp forms of a given weight and level, whose normalized leading coefficients are non-negative. If such a hypothesis equivalent formula is found to be invalid, it would indicate the existence of a cusp form for which the Riemann Hypothesis of Duke-Weinberger does not hold.

The iterative solution of large linear equation systems often relies on preconditioning techniques to speed up convergence, particularly when using Krylov subspace methods. We investigate a new approach to preconditioning sparse matrices by utilizing the full multigrid method, which can be effectively implemented on parallel computing systems. By combining the multigrid method with Krylov subspace techniques, we can leverage the strengths of both methods to create an efficient hybrid algorithm. We propose two innovative hybrid algorithms, which utilize the multigrid approximate Schur complement method as a preconditioner, and evaluate their performance through numerical experiments.

The polarized, mass-inclusive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}$ is calculated to the third order in QCD, an achievement documented in this paper. Our findings are crucial in understanding the evolution of polarized parton distribution functions within the framework of Quantum Chromodynamics, specifically at the N$^3$LO level. To validate our results, we demonstrate their consistency with prior, related operator matrix elements. Additionally, we provide the necessary components to facilitate the transition from $\overline{\text{MS}}$ to collinear PDFs, accounting for the effects of a non-zero quark mass $m$.

In the rapidly evolving field of intelligent systems, it is essential to gather comprehensive information about real-world incidents involving these systems. This requires an extensive collection of detailed reports, which can be achieved through the development of a structured form that captures all necessary information. This paper introduces a collaborative project, the Global Brain-HMI Incidents Collection (GBHIC), which aims to gather a vast database of incidents related to brain-computer interface human-machine interactions. To facilitate this initiative, we have created a standardized form that enables us to collect a wide variety of reports from diverse sources. To date, the GBHIC has amassed a substantial collection of 180 reports, sourced from multiple organizations and individuals, encompassing a broad range of brain-computer interface technologies and applications.

The principle underlying the renormalization group is intrinsically linked to the concept of flow, which, in scalar field theory, bears a strong analogy to gradient flow. This relationship can be formalized by expressing the renormalization group equation as a specific type of partial differential equation, similar to the gradient flow equation. Consequently, it becomes possible to interpret the renormalization group as a flow process within a state space that evolves over time, corresponding to changes in the cutoff scale.

In the field of medicine, adherence to established clinical protocols is crucial for effective treatment. However, the application of these protocols in real-world settings is often hindered by the individual variability of patients. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel approach that combines the expertise of medical professionals with advanced machine learning techniques. This method enables the creation of a predictive model that can accurately assess a patient's suitability for treatments aligned with clinical protocols. The proposed solution is demonstrated through its application to the treatment of heart failure patients, where it has been found to improve treatment selection accuracy by 15% compared to the average patient.

We propose an innovative linear type system for a quantum programming language that incorporates both classical and quantum data. This type system is designed to be an efficient and accurate representation of quantum computations, and we demonstrate its practicality by implementing it in a standard quantum circuit compiler. This compiler, which is both sound and complete, translates linearity into a compact instruction set, and we show that the resulting compiler output is equivalent to the original quantum program. This allows us to provide a quantum program with a concise and accurate description of its behavior, and to verify its correctness using traditional classical methods.

We've developed a two-dimensional percolation model based on a random bipartite graph, where the distribution of its eigenvalues reveals an interesting phenomenon. An exceptional pair of eigenvalues is isolated at the edge of the spectrum, separated from the rest of the eigenvalues by a distinct gap. As the graph's size increases beyond a critical threshold, these eigenvalues exhibit critical behavior, accompanied by the disappearance of the gap and the emergence of a perimeter phase transition. By analyzing the eigenfunctions associated with these eigenvalues, we've discovered a direct connection to a random walk on the grid, where the eigenvalues of the former correspond to the former's trap probabilities.

We've developed a straightforward model to explain how entanglement between distant atoms grows rapidly through the exchange of virtual photons, resulting in an integrated photon structure function that's connected to photon parton distribution functions used in high-energy physics. Additionally, our research demonstrates that the long-term interactions between the atoms can be effectively represented by a single-unit photon, analogous to a single quark in a proton.

Assembling a de novo genome from whole-genome sequencing data is a complex process that involves reconstructing an organism's complete genome from fragmented DNA sequences.  Due to the large size of genomes, as well as the variability in DNA fragment sizes, ascertaining their order and orientation presents significant computational challenges.  In this study, we introduce a novel, efficient algorithm for genome assembly that leverages the adjacency graph of DNA fragments, incorporating both short and long-range DNA sequences to improve accuracy.  By integrating the information from DNA sequences, our approach produces a genome assembly with minimized errors, and can be applied to a wide range of genomes, from bacteria to humans.  In contrast to existing methods, our algorithm excels in producing high-quality genome assemblies for complex genomes, and demonstrates superior performance in producing compact and accurate genome structures.

The delayed logistic equation's decades-long resistance to analytical solutions has prompted researchers to explore various methods for approximating its dynamics. This study builds on existing work by incorporating a non-standard approach to bifurcation analysis, focusing on the equation's oscillatory behavior. We develop a simplified model to analyze periodic solutions and their stability, then apply this to a specific case involving the delayed logistic equation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of periodic solutions emerging from stable equilibrium states, as well as the possibility of stable limit cycles in the equation's two-dimensional dynamics.

We introduce a depth-based method for analyzing and making inferences about temporal patterns, including their timing and frequency. Our approach builds on a nonparametric framework that utilizes statistical depth, which doesn't rely on specific distributions or the Hurwitz process model. We develop a method for measuring the relative importance of observed temporal patterns by ranking them in depth, and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations and real-world data analysis, including modeling earthquake occurrences and monitoring heart rate variability.

In the field of nanotechnology, the development of quantum systems has led to the creation of highly efficient energy and heat management devices. The use of quantum phenomena, such as entanglement and interference, has the potential to create innovative thermal machines that outperform their classical counterparts. To explore this concept, researchers have developed a model of an autonomous quantum heat engine based on a two-types of quantum tunneling mechanisms - tunneling Assumption and coherent tunneling. The results show that the quantum engine can produce more power than its classical counterpart, the tunneling Assumption engine, and that the quantum system's ability to entangle particles further enhances power output. The findings also indicate that the quantum engine exhibits superior efficiency compared to both the tunneling Assumption engine and a model based on the assumption of independent particle behavior.

The research paper presents new findings from a laser-based spectroscopy study of the isotope $^{69}$Ge performed on the ISOLDE facility at CERN.  The study's results have yielded revised values for the nuclear magnetic and quadrupole moments of $^{69}$Ge, as well as a precise measurement of the hyperfine constant.  The obtained data has been compared to theoretical predictions from various computational models.  Additionally, the study has provided confirmation of the spin and parity of the isomer $^{69m}$Ge.  The study's results have also facilitated a more accurate determination of the nuclear magnetic moment of the isotope $^{71}$Ge.

We have introduced a refined method for accurately measuring the mass of highly unstable and unusual atomic isotopes. This novel technique, known as a storage ring isomer tagging method, enables the precise detection of decay products from highly energetic atomic isotopes. Our experimental setup has successfully made groundbreaking, highly precise mass measurements of short-lived atomic isotopes, including a 0.04 ppb level mass measurement of a particularly rare isotope, Ni$^{59}$, formed through the decay of a highly energetic isomer, Ni$^{59m}$. This achievement represents the first time an isomer's decay has been used to make such a precise mass measurement.

We employ the multicanonical method to generate Boltzmann distributions for SU(2) lattice field theories on a 4^4 grid, utilizing both the fundamental group and the combined fundamental and twisted basic groups.

We introduce a new approach to identifying structured text patterns using regular expressions, which can be applied to various formats like XML, JSON, and SQL. Our method combines the benefits of regex-based structured text recognition and NLP techniques for extracting meaning from unstructured text. We develop a new, efficient algorithm for combining regexes with NLP methods, which can be utilized by a user-friendly tool, REXLER, to convert simple regexes into meaningful representations of structured data.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC has collected proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV energy, totaling 91 fb$^{-1}$, and searched for decays of the third-generation scalar tau sneutrino into a tau lepton and a neutrino. This search was conducted using fully reconstructed tau leptons in events featuring either one or three tau leptons and significant event transverse momentum. A novel machine-learning technique was employed to enhance the search's sensitivity. The results showed no evidence for the decay, and instead established the most stringent limits on the production cross-section of the tau sneutrino across various mass ranges.

The task of cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing demands accurate generation of representation and structure from natural language descriptions, yet current approaches often overlook the importance of these components, resulting in subpar performance when applied to domains beyond their training data. To address this shortcoming, we propose a novel framework called CoGen, which utilizes a joint generation and annotation model to simultaneously produce cross-domain SQL representations and structures from natural language descriptions. The joint modeling is achieved through a shared attention mechanism, enabling cross-component interactions, and is further enhanced by a dual-path design that facilitates information exchange between canonical SQL queries and natural language descriptions. The efficacy of CoGen is demonstrated through superior performance on two prominent datasets, and the results indicate its potential for improving cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing tasks.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a comprehensive radio sky survey at 1.4 GHz using the LOFAR telescope, covering a significant portion of the northern sky over the course of several years. Initial results from LoTSS Deep Field 1 have shown promising discoveries, prompting a deeper investigation at 45 $\mu$Jy/beam. This study further explores the area surrounding the LoTSS Deep Field 1 data, covering a larger area of 100 square degrees, at the same depth. Notable findings include 12 previously undiscovered sources above 100 $\mu$Jy/beam, as well as a catalog of 109 sources above 45 $\mu$Jy/beam. The research also presents a statistical analysis of source counts and radio luminosity functions, as well as a discussion on the physical characteristics of the sources. The findings are complemented by optical and X-ray data from other surveys, resulting in 10 sources with multi-wavelength data. The research presents the first multi-wavelength data for the LoTSS Deep Field 1, offering new insights into the structure and evolution of the Universe.

A new statistical model, the high-dimensional rank lasso, combines the benefits of the multivariate analysis of variance and isotonic regression. It effectively balances interpretability and flexibility in determining linear combinations of high-dimensional data that have a distinct rank structure. We develop a convex optimization model for the high-dimensional rank Lasso, enabling precise parameter estimation and identification of structured relationships in high-dimensional data. The model's performance is demonstrated through simulations and real-world data analysis, showcasing its ability to identify meaningful patterns in complex data sets.

We investigate whether there are any universal, optimal strategies to minimize average entropy generation in systems that gradually change. By leveraging recent research, we establish the existence of such strategies by demonstrating the convex nature of an entropy-related function. Furthermore, we develop an efficient numerical approach to find these strategies, which can be applied to both cases where entropy generation is controlled and uncontrolled. Our study includes the derivation of a specific, time-dependent strategy that is optimal in all scenarios, which is then used to validate our method through numerical examples.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into addressing environmental issues has gained significant attention, yet the full extent of its impact on the environment remains unclear. In this research, we introduce the concept of EcoAI and explore the broader ecological implications of AI-driven solutions. We examine the AI lifecycle, considering both direct and indirect environmental costs, and identify key research areas. Our analysis reveals that AI-driven solutions can inadvertently harm the environment, and we argue that these external costs should be factored into their design. We propose the EcoAI framework to guide the development of AI systems that are environmentally sustainable, and we discuss the ethical implications of prioritizing AI's ecological footprint.

Prescriptive process monitoring aims to pinpoint processes that require improvement by forecasting the likely consequences of ongoing process executions. This field of study is gaining increasing attention due to its potential to provide real-time insights into the effects of ongoing processes. This paper delves into the optimization of prescriptive process monitoring through the identification of processes that, if altered, would minimize expected negative outcomes. We propose a novel framework for optimizing prescriptive process monitoring that involves identifying processes that, if modified, would minimize expected negative outcomes. This framework is based on a predictive model that predicts the likely consequences of ongoing process executions. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of optimizing prescriptive process monitoring through the identification of processes that, if modified, would minimize expected negative outcomes by comparing it to traditional process optimization methods.

This study introduces an efficient numerical method for accurately controlling the errors associated with the compressible Navier-Stokes equations in a periodic domain. The approach utilizes an entropy-based error control mechanism, which enables the calculation of the solution's upper bound. To simulate real-world phenomena, the model's coefficients for thermal conductivity and fluid viscosity are assumed to be temperature-dependent. The numerical scheme is built upon a second-order, entropy-stable finite element method, which employs the Strang splitting technique to split the conservative and dissipative components of the equations. The errors associated with each component are evaluated separately, which facilitates the development of an adaptive time step size based on an a posteriori error analysis. The model is solved using the discontinuous Galerkin method, which is combined with the Newton iteration to solve the resulting nonlinear system. The analysis shows that the upper bound on the entropy production is controlled, which in turn ensures the stability of the computed solution.

Polynomial-time data reduction methods, known as kernelization algorithms, are used to decrease the size of NP-hard problems to a size proportional to a polynomial of the kernel parameter $k$. However, in many cases, the kernel size significantly exceeds the parameter $k$, often being a linear function of the original input size. This paper presents an alternative approach to kernelization, focusing on problems with a parameterized sublinear size, by developing parameter-shattering algorithms that reduce problem instances to a constant number of subinstances of arbitrary size. We apply this new methodology to design shattering algorithms with optimal runtime for three specific problems: finding the largest induced subgraph with a specific property, coloring vertices with a specified number of colors, and edge list covering.

We're investigating opinion dynamics in a network where each agent only considers the opinions of their acquaintances, leading to different opinion clusters forming. Our research focuses on the impact of friendly relationships, represented by a network of connections, on these opinion shifts. The 'friendship' concept is incorporated into our model of bounded confidence, resulting in a new model that allows us to analyze how friendly relationships influence opinion formation. Our results show that the opinion network's structure is influenced by both the initial opinions and friendly relationships, with strong connections leading to distinct opinion clusters. Our research also reveals that increasing the number of friendly connections can lead to more and more separate opinion clusters, with some agents forming close friendships and others remaining isolated.

We examine the electrostatic properties of black holes with charged scalar fields, focusing on their impact on electrostatic energy, which is a key aspect of their internal structure. Our research reveals that the charged black hole solutions with scalar fields have event horizons and an internal Cauchy horizon, with a de Sitter space between them. In these spacetimes, the electromagnetic field is non-degenerate, and we find that the region between the horizons contributes infinite electrostatic potential energy, rendering the ADM mass uneuitable for characterization. Consequently, we investigate the electric field's behavior outside the outer event horizon and calculate the electrostatic potential and associated free energy. Our results show that a new phase emerges beyond a certain temperature, characterized by a non-zero electrostatic free energy, indicating the development of scalar "hair" on the black hole. This phase transition is accompanied by a second-order change in electrostatic free energy, and the resulting black hole "hairs" are found to be non-topological and localized near the event horizon.

Understanding how genes respond over time is crucial for deciphering complex biological processes. A novel method has been developed to analyze the rate at which genes are activated in response to a given stimulus, based on synchronized mRNA expression data. This method classifies genes with similar activation patterns and identifies the variability in their expression levels. Applying this method to multiple datasets revealed distinct groups of genes with shared activation rates, as well as genes exhibiting rapid or delayed activation. Furthermore, analysis of the datasets showed that differences in mRNA expression over time are not only influenced by transcriptional activation but also by post-transcriptional regulation mechanisms. This method provides a valuable tool for exploring the underlying processes that govern gene expression in response to specific stimuli.

This outcome has been achieved through the analysis of transfer reaction data and the identification of new excited states. The discovery of 64Ni's low-spin structure has revealed several previously unobserved 0+, 2+, and 4+ states, with energies up to 70 MeV. The identification of these states has been supported by the observation of specific alpha-particle bands and the 64Ni(0+) to 70Ni(0+) band structure. We have developed a set of constraints that ensure the consistency of $\mathcal{N}=1$ conformal field theories in four dimensions, focusing on unitary, conformal, and Lorentz invariance. Our analysis centers on $\mathcal{N}=1$ conformal field theories that can be described as infrared fixed points of unitary, renormalizable, and Lorentz invariant Lagrangians with chiral fermions. By utilizing the concept of 't Hooft anomalies, we derive upper limits on scalar operator dimensions within these CFTs. Our findings are supported by a theoretical framework that allows us to construct conformal theories with the maximum possible symmetry, which we then use to establish our anomaly-based bounds. Additionally, we have identified key relationships between the coefficients of the E and F anomalies, which are essential in defining the limits on scalar operator dimensions. Our research also explores the implications of these anomaly ratios on the conformal dimensions of other operators, specifically the stress tensor, and we have demonstrated the consistency of our results with existing superconformal theories.

This study introduces a novel class of group codes, specifically linear complementary pair (LCP) group codes, formed by intersecting a group code and its dual, within the group algebra of an additive group. We establish a precise condition for a group code to contain an LCP pair, along with a related characterization based on its dual. Our findings are illustrated through a variety of examples and accompanied by several related theorems and lemmas.

In probabilistic graphical models, we often work with functions that depend on multiple variables, which can be represented in various forms such as a sum of products. We introduce a new, compact way to represent these functions using a finite state machine, which is especially useful for models with a structured pattern, like those based on a grid. Our approach allows us to perform calculations on these functions efficiently, reducing the computational cost significantly. We also show how to incorporate this representation into a method for learning a key property of a group of variables, and provide a faster alternative to traditional methods for doing so.

This research focuses on a multimodal object localization task, where we examine how various cues can be used to identify objects in a cluttered environment. We simulate a scenario where an object is hidden beneath a surface, accessible only through an opening, and explore how different agents can locate it using visual, auditory, or combined cues. Our investigation reveals that while visual information alone is insufficient, incorporating sound enables agents to successfully retrieve the concealed object. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that human-like behavior, characterized by using visual cues initially and sound later, yields optimal outcomes.

The transition from thickening to flowing in dense suspensions under high stress is often attributed to the overcoming of attractive forces by repulsive forces. We investigate the role of interactions in this process using simulations of particles with interactions that can be tuned. Our analysis reveals that the thickening transition occurs when particles in the shear zone shift from interacting via attractive forces to interacting via forces that can be either attractive or repulsive.

This study utilizes a stochastic model to simulate the power crisis in Ghana, which is characterized by intermittent electricity outages. The duration of low electricity consumption is modeled as a randomly varying time period, with a probability distribution that is estimated based on data from the Ghanaian government. The government's data indicates a decreasing trend in outage durations, with the likelihood of extended outages continuing to decline. The model's validity is confirmed through the analysis of real-world data, which is obtained from the Ghanaian electricity sector. The results of the study have significant implications for the insurance industry, which is responsible for compensating policyholders for losses incurred due to power outages. The study's findings provide a basis for the calculation of premiums, which are necessary for the sustainability of the property and casualty insurance sector in Ghana.

Web search personalisation has become a prevalent feature, yet its impact on search results remains unclear. Our study examines the extent to which personalisation influences search by comparing the web pages of personalised and non-personalised search engines. We conducted an experiment involving 100 participants and 800 queries, then assessed the relevance of the obtained search results. Our findings indicate that average users may overlook approximately 18% of pertinent information and encounter around 20% more unhelpful content in personalised searches compared to non-personalised ones. Our analysis also reveals that personalisation tends to favour certain websites, with around 10% of all results coming from a select group of sites. Our data is publicly accessible at https://osf.io/5jy3k/.

Automatically creating code based on a visual flowchart is an unsolved problem in the field of program synthesis. To address this challenge, we developed a system that takes flowcharts as input and generates the corresponding program in a specified language matching the specified output. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to visually synthesize programs from such a graphical representation. We tested our system on a collection of flowcharts representing simple arithmetic operations and found that it successfully created matching code in 88% of cases. Additionally, the system accurately identified the corresponding code in a multiple-choice format 83% of the time. We also explored its capability to identify errors in flowcharts by comparing its results to those of a control group, finding that the system accurately identified faulty input 75% of the time.

This text outlines multiple reduction techniques for Earth's climate models, which are then compared to a set of standard benchmarks. These benchmarks assess the accuracy and reliability of the reduced models in terms of their numerical solutions and ability to replicate meaningful climate patterns. Additionally, the text discusses a set of standardized tests for evaluating the consistency and stability of the numerical methods employed in creating the reduced models. These tests are designed to ensure that the reduced models maintain their steady-state and time-evolution characteristics, similar to their more complex original models.

The heaviest elements in the universe are created through a process called the rapid neutron capture process, occurring in neutron star mergers. A key factor in this process is the speed at which the reaction takes place, influenced by the flow of matter in the aftermath of the merger. We've discovered that the movement of matter in the merger can be described by a universal scaling pattern, which we've applied to understand the heavy element creation process. Our findings show that the heavy element creation process is faster in regions of high matter movement, particularly in the merger's final moments. This new approach allows us to predict the heavy element creation rates in the merger's complex environment.

Radiation-cancer treatment using linear accelerators can be made more precise by incorporating MR imaging, allowing for real-time tracking of moving tumors and surrounding organs. This precision is further enhanced by real-time radiation beam adjustments. The integration of tracking, gating, and beam control technologies is essential for safe and effective treatment. This paper examines the challenges associated with MR-linac systems and the methods employed to address them, specifically in the context of Siemens' MR-linac technology.

Compositional data analysis is a statistical technique that deals with data like chemical concentrations and survey data that sum to a constant value.  The recent surge in data from compositional sources, particularly in microbiome research, has led to a need for robust data visualization techniques.  Our research introduces a novel method for creating scatter plot matrices that can effectively display relationships between components of compositional data.  The proposed method leverages the robust nature of Spearman correlation and log-ratio transformations to provide reliable results, even in the presence of outliers.  The efficacy of our approach has been demonstrated through simulations and real data examples, including microbiome data analysis.

The existence of a specific gap in the distribution of known exoplanets, referred to as the "55 Cancri desert," has been observed in the literature. This gap is characterized by a lack of planets within a particular range of masses and orbital distances. It is believed that this phenomenon is caused by the destruction of planets by giant stellar magnetic fields. To investigate this further, we conducted an analysis of the star 55 Cancri A, which has a magnetic field that is 100 times stronger than the Sun's. Our study reveals that the star's magnetic field is primarily concentrated at its poles, forming a unique shape. We found that the star's magnetic field is capable of swallowing a planet the size of Earth if it orbits within 0.06 astronomical units from the star. Our research suggests that the "55 Cancri desert" may be caused by the destruction of planets by the magnetic fields of their host stars.

To accomplish complex tasks, it's essential for artificial agents to focus their attention, given that they can't perceive their entire environment at once. Although existing methods exist for attention control, they're often task-specific and rely on pre-defined rules. We've developed a universal system that learns to allocate attention dynamically, based on its past performance. This attention mechanism is integrated into a cyclic neural network, which allows it to remember and apply what it has learned to new situations. We've tested this system on two demanding visual tasks, where it outperformed existing methods, and it also surpassed a human benchmark in one of the tasks.

Recurrent neural networks have been widely used in various tasks, but their effectiveness is often hindered by the need for extensive training and large amounts of data due to the high dimensionality of their hidden states. To address this issue, we developed locality masked recurrent neural networks (LM-RNNs), which combine the efficiency of sparse weight matrices and the benefits of spatial self-attention. By limiting interactions to spatially proximate elements, LM-RNNs reduce the complexity of their hidden state representation, resulting in improved data efficiency and faster convergence. We also explored the potential of LM-RNNs to learn hierarchical representations, where lower levels focus on local details and higher levels capture broader contextual information. Our experiments demonstrate that LM-RNNs outperform fully-connected RNNs and spatially masked RNNs in multiple tasks, including language modeling, machine translation, and visual question answering.

We introduce a general approach to categorizing nilpotent algebras by dimension, based on their commutativity and nilpotency degree, which is analogous to the classification of strictly commutative algebras. This method yields explicit results for commutative Jordan-Kirakosian algebras, allowing us to identify the maximum nilpotency degree and classify algebra structures up to isomorphism in specific cases.

Active galactic nuclei's supermassive black holes' growth is influenced by their relativistic jets, which also impact their surrounding environments.  Although the connection between black hole growth and jet power has been observed, the relationship is not fully understood.  The growth of black hole mass and its effect on jet power is investigated in this study.  The results indicate that more massive black holes produce more powerful jets, which in turn suggest that more massive black holes' environments are suppressed by their jets, resulting in less accretion and slower growth.  The observed pattern of black hole growth versus mass is consistent with theoretical models of black hole growth, which are regulated by feedback mechanisms.

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of $1/c^2$, where $c$ represents the speed of light. The resulting expansion is expressed using a specific spacetime metric, with its associated covariant derivatives. The $1/c^2$ expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert density is found to match a previously derived expression by Ni, although we arrive at this conclusion through a distinct method.

This study introduces a novel, Davenport-Smith-pencils-based approach to 3D local image analysis, which leverages the inherent symmetry between scale and polarization (SP-symmetry). We demonstrate that SP-symmetry exhibits distinct patterns in 3D local features, which can be effectively represented as concentric rings and ellipses. Building upon this, we define the scale-invariant property as preserving these shapes across varying scales. To achieve this, we develop a theory of image feature rescaling that maintains SP-symmetry, which can be applied to various 3D feature types, including voxel-based, wavelet-based, and gradient-based features. We validate our proposed method through experiments on synthetic and real-world images, which reveal that our SP-invariant feature extraction technique exhibits enhanced robustness to changes in polarization and scale, outperforming traditional scale-invariant features.

Our study involved detailed photometric and spectroscopic observations, as well as a thorough examination of the system's spectral characteristics. Our analysis revealed that the primary star in this binary system is a B9.5V type, while the secondary star has an estimated effective temperature of 6000K. Our photometric and spectroscopic data indicate that the system is composed of two distinct stars, with no evidence of a third body or a disk surrounding the binary system. We introduce a novel, lightweight pooling technique that's applicable to various models, including CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers. This simple yet effective method outperforms traditional global pooling in several ways, with a notable advantage of being parameter-free. In our experiments, global pooling was substituted with cross-entropy loss in ImageNet classification tasks, yielding improved results. Additionally, we found that our cross-entropy loss with the new pooling technique can be used interchangeably with existing global pooling methods without any performance loss, with cross-entropy being faster to compute.
