This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the four-dimensional Euclidean space, specifically those that are flat and exhibit a constant, non-zero, regular slope. We identify the non-planar, flat general rotation surfaces that possess constant curvature lines, and we demonstrate that a Clifford torus is the sole surface with constant principal curvature lines among all flat general rotational surfaces.

Deep neural networks that perform semantic segmentation are typically trained using large datasets with precisely marked images. This process is costly and requires extensive manual annotation. To alleviate this burden, we've developed an approach to pre-train a segmentation model by using depth information from videos that don't need to be annotated. This method involves using depth maps from various scenes to initially train a model that can understand relationships between pixels, and then use this model to perform a task that involves predicting class probabilities for each pixel. This model can then be adapted to a new target scene with just a few annotated frames. To evaluate our approach, we've created a new dataset called SceneFlow-SEG, which combines existing video datasets with segmentation masks for specific scenes. This allows us to test our model on a variety of new environments. Experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms existing approaches that rely on target-domain annotations, and only slightly lags behind models that have access to extensive target-domain annotations.

Time-series data visualization is essential in numerous fields, yet effectively conveying complex time-series data through a compelling narrative remains a significant challenge. The sheer volume of time-series data and the diverse expertise required to interpret it can make manual analysis and interpretation impractical. To address this issue, we've developed a tool called TCube, which automatically generates a 3D interactive visualization of multiple time-series data sets, accompanied by a coherent and informative story. TCube leverages cutting-edge machine learning and natural language processing to create a customized, data-driven narrative that highlights key patterns and insights. TCube has been successfully applied to real-world data in fields like medicine and industry, and our findings demonstrate its potential to facilitate the efficient and accurate analysis of large time-series data sets by making them more accessible and understandable.

The LHCb experiment at CERN has made significant advancements in the study of particle and antimatter asymmetries, focusing on specific meson decays. Notable results include the measurement of CP asymmetry in the B0d meson and analysis of B+ and B0s mesons' rare decay processes. These findings contribute to our understanding of the fundamental laws governing the universe.
On a Cayley tree, we examine the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups.

This study examines the smooth solutions to a specific type of hyperbolic equation in four dimensions, where the coefficients experience a slight explosion. We demonstrate that the solution's coefficients exhibit a specific growth pattern, where the explosion rate can be arbitrarily slowed by adjusting a parameter. This result expands upon previous research by Mitrea and Tataru and is partially based on an idea proposed by Alinhac.

Japanese word segmentation poses a more complex challenge than Chinese word segmentation due to the absence of word boundaries in continuous Japanese text.  To address this challenge, a new approach has been developed that leverages Chinese word segmentation techniques, by translating Japanese text into Chinese using a neural machine translation model.  This innovative method outperforms existing Japanese word segmentation models, achieving significant improvements in accuracy, particularly for shorter text samples.

On Stack Overflow, users can reference external knowledge by linking to other pages. Although the platform's policy permits external links, their usefulness is debatable. This study investigates the prevalence and characteristics of external links used by Stack Overflow users. We gathered data on all questions and answers from Stack Overflow, examining both the frequency of external knowledge references and the types of online resources linked to. Our analysis reveals that a significant portion of external links point to programming-related online resources, with a notable lack of connections to general knowledge sites. Furthermore, external links are primarily used in questions, with users rarely referencing them in answers.

We've conducted an extensive analysis of 128 galaxy clusters, sourced from the XXL, COSMOS, and ELAIS-N1 fields, to investigate the properties of Self-Interacting Dark Matter. Our research focused on the central core sizes of these clusters, revealing that the majority of the 100 clusters with significant signal exhibited core sizes exceeding 200 kpc. This finding is inconsistent with the predictions of standard cold dark matter models, which suggest minimal core sizes of less than 100 kpc. Furthermore, our results indicate that the sensitivity of the dark matter core sizes to the influence of baryonic feedback is lower than previously thought for certain models of dark matter particle interactions.

Climate change communication is essential, yet many climate change messages fail to resonate.  This study examines the climate change communication literature to identify strategies that can improve how people understand and act on the issue.  We focus on a specific type of research that analyzes the effectiveness of various communication methods through surveys or experiments.  Our analysis reveals that the literature is still in its early stages, with limited research on the most effective ways to communicate climate change.  We find that the literature is heavily influenced by Western, educated, industrialized, and democratic countries, leaving other regions underrepresented.  We also find that the literature is dominated by researchers in social sciences, with climate scientists and communicators underrepresented.  As a result, the literature is limited in its understanding of the most effective ways to communicate climate change.  To address these limitations, we suggest that researchers collaborate across disciplines and regions to develop more effective climate change communication strategies.

Clinical symptoms are crucial indicators of a patient's health, yet their accurate detection in electronic health records is complicated by the diverse ways symptoms are documented. To address this challenge, we developed a technique that leverages institutional-specific cues to accurately identify symptoms in patient notes. By training on data from multiple hospitals, our approach is also robust to variations between institutions. To verify its effectiveness, we established a large, multi-institutional dataset comprising 17,000 patient notes from 7 different hospitals, each with distinct documentation styles. The results of our experiments show that this technique significantly improves symptom identification compared to a baseline model, particularly when applied to notes from hospitals not included in the training data.

Deep reinforcement learning has shown promise in addressing the challenge of supervised learning in autonomous driving, primarily due to its ability to generate realistic driving data. However, the issue of domain shift between training and testing environments poses a significant obstacle. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a domain-independent driving simulation called DriveKit, which is designed to be easily modified and adaptable. Our solution involves using domain-invariant features as targets for both supervised learning and deep reinforcement learning, thereby enabling models to generalize across different domains. We validate DriveKit's effectiveness through comparison with deep reinforcement learning baselines and demonstrate its ability to adapt to new domains without prior exposure.

Deep learning has proven to be highly effective in solving complex problems, but it has a significant drawback: its reliance on Artificial Neural Networks results in high computational costs and substantial energy consumption. In response, researchers have developed an alternative architecture known as Spiking Neural Networks, which mimics the behavior of living neurons and synapses. ANN-based models can be reinterpreted as Leaky Integrate-and-Fire neurons, thereby enabling their deployment on Spiking Neural Networks hardware for more efficient processing. This paper explores the potential of leveraging specialized SNN hardware to accelerate the inference of existing AI models, with a focus on facial recognition. By demonstrating the feasibility of this approach, we aim to highlight the value of innovative hardware design in addressing the energy efficiency challenges of deep learning.

This study examines the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, using a two-flavor NJL model. We focus on neutral matter, where the polarization of the strange quark naturally remains zero. By analyzing the quark energy levels in a confined space, we can calculate key thermodynamic properties, such as pressure, energy density, and speed of sound, and compare them to those of neutral strange stars.

A significant number of devices, including smartphones and laptops, are frequently underutilized, presenting an opportunity to leverage their spare computing power.  By utilizing volunteer computing systems, such as Pando, these systems can run distributed applications across a network of volunteer-powered servers.  These distributed applications can be particularly beneficial for resource-intensive tasks, like data analysis and machine learning, which often require significant computational resources.  This study presents a set of findings from testing the suitability of the Python programming language for running these resource-heavy applications on Pando-powered clusters, by evaluating a variety of Python libraries in comparison to C++ for use in parallel and distributed applications.

A new approach to solving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, based on an existing framework for dealing with non-linear equations. By converting the eigenvalue problem into a matrix equation, a large system of equations can be formed, which can then be solved iteratively using a solution refinement technique. To speed up convergence, a minimum point estimation method is employed, utilizing data from previous iterations to generate approximations to the solution. The proposed technique has been successfully tested on a real-world application, the simulation of light propagation in optical fibers, and demonstrated significant improvements in convergence speed, often reaching speeds comparable to existing specialized methods.

We show that the intermediate beta-transformations with a multiplicative base, when a hole is present at zero, can be topologically linked to the greedy beta-transformations with a hole at zero. This connection allows us to explore the topology of interval maps that result from applying these beta-transformations with a hole. Additionally, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between certain classes of intermediate beta-transformations and greedy beta-transformations, both with a hole at zero, based on their symbolic sequences.

We've discovered that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and matter fields represented as vectors confine through monopole condensation, causing the symmetries of chiral and global $Z_{2}$ to break down. Our findings are based on an analysis of the theory's magnetic dual, which has an anisotropic scalar field with a distinct potential.

Machine learning models, particularly tree ensembles, are favored for their predictive capabilities, yet they are often criticized for being overly complex and difficult to interpret. To address this criticism, we've developed a new method called Disentangled Attribution Curves, which provides clear and understandable explanations for predictions made by these models. This method excels at pinpointing crucial time points and accurately ranking the importance of input variables, and our experiments show that it outperforms existing attribution methods in time series forecasting models, with tree-based projections exhibiting the most promising results.

Recent advancements in federated learning have garnered significant interest for its capability to address privacy concerns. Nevertheless, the confidentiality of local model updates remains uncertain, potentially allowing malicious participants to surreptitiously transmit their model updates to the aggregator, thereby compromising the confidentiality of their training data. To address this shortcoming, we have developed an aggregator, called PrivAgg, that can process model updates from a Trusted Execution Environment, thereby safeguarding the privacy of federated learning. To further bolster the confidentiality of the learning process, we have created a secure protocol that enables model aggregation within a Trusted Execution Environment, protecting both the model updates and the aggregation process from eavesdroppers. To mitigate the performance disparity among edge devices, we have designed an innovative aggregation method, called Quantized Average, that can effectively consolidate model updates from edge devices with varying capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that our aggregator, PrivAgg, surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art aggregators, while also achieving superior accuracy and convergence speed compared to traditional aggregators.

The interaction between embedded software and external devices often leads to complex issues in testing and debugging, a common challenge in the embedded systems field. This problem is particularly prevalent in industries like automotive, where safety-critical systems are prevalent. This study presents an innovative approach to test embedded systems by utilizing a test chip that simulates external devices. The test chip is designed to be compatible with various microcontroller units, making it versatile for different applications. The test chip is currently being used to test critical functions in automotive systems, showcasing its practical value. This research outlines the motivation behind the test chip, its architecture, and the methods for test case development.

Most cloud-based system call filtering methods rely on static analysis, which is ineffective for cloud applications that dynamically create threads. This research introduces a novel, runtime feedback loop called Timeloops, which uses actual microservices behavior to establish a call graph and an allowed system call filter. This approach is demonstrated through a microservices example and evaluated on real-world applications, showing that Timeloops outperforms static analysis in producing more accurate filters and surpasses existing dynamic filtering methods in terms of system overhead and filter accuracy.

We have developed a unified framework for linear classification in metric product spaces, regardless of their geometric properties. Our framework demonstrates that, irrespective of the curvature, pairs of identical distributions can be efficiently transformed into data sets that can be perfectly classified by a linear classifier. Additionally, we have proven that all projected linear classifiers possess the same capacity for representing complex data, which can be learned through standard optimization techniques. Our findings also imply that certain distribution separation tasks are inherently limitable by three-dimensional geometries. Finally, our research provides a theoretical justification for the success of linearity-inducing transformations in high-dimensional data sets, as well as the use of lines and hyperplanes in deep learning models.

This introduction focuses on stochastic Model Predictive Control methods that account for uncertainty in constraints, illustrated through a linear system under unpredictable conditions. The accompanying lecture serves as an accessible entry point to the subject, complementing more comprehensive references that delve deeper into its complexities.

The concept of compressive learning, which integrates sensing and data analysis, has been used to create efficient data collection methods.  However, the complexity of the learning process can be a major obstacle, particularly when dealing with large-scale problems.  This paper presents a new framework for addressing this issue by leveraging the sparse characteristics of data and its underlying structure.  By combining these elements, we can significantly reduce the computational demands of learning.  This framework incorporates a novel approach to projection, which enables us to develop fast algorithms for solving complex problems.  These algorithms are based on iterative methods and can be used to solve a variety of learning tasks, including regression and classification.  Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that these algorithms converge rapidly and achieve high levels of accuracy.  Experimental results show that the proposed framework outperforms existing solutions in terms of both computational efficiency and accuracy.

A mathematical model of two species competition is developed, taking into account species dispersal between a finite number of areas, resulting in a system of reaction-diffusion equations. The model's global dynamics are analyzed, and it is proven that the system has a unique positive steady state, which is also stable. Furthermore, a condition is established that determines whether one species will outcompete the other, influenced by initial conditions and global parameters, with immigration having a more significant impact than diffusion.

We examine abelian quantum double models, a class of exactly solvable spin systems, where we prove that the local structure of each frustration-free ground state over a convex area corresponds to a von Neumann algebra of type $II_{\infty}$.

To enhance magnon-photon-photon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we suggest a novel setup that involves a two-terminal nanowire nanoresonator situated within a cavity and coupled with a co-propagating three-level nanowire nanocavities system. The system's internal components, a SQUID and a two-terminal nanowire nanoresonator, interact through a sophisticated coupling mechanism. The extraordinary properties of one-dimensional nanowires enable the system to achieve exceptional entanglement levels, as evidenced by our theoretical findings.

We've derived one-loop triple-collinear splitting matrices for color and spin spaces, considering all possible scenarios, within massless QCD theory. Our results are expressed in a dimensionless format and are applicable across various dimensional spaces. The splitting matrices are written in terms of a dimensionless form factor, which is specific to a color configuration and has $J$ helicity. This form factor is related to a particular type of scattering amplitude, and we've obtained its one-loop expression.

A general Neron Desingularization has been established for one-dimensional local rings, and this principle has been utilized to demonstrate Neron's criterion for excellent rings in its cohomological formulation.

The daily movement of the Sun has long been a significant source of inspiration for scientific inquiry, a fascination that has persisted throughout human history. In the era of classical Islamic civilization, the Sun's movement played a vital role in both religious and scientific pursuits, prompting the development of a sophisticated system of timekeeping based on shadows. This system, known as astrolabe time, was refined and documented in numerous scientific treatises, which in turn laid the groundwork for the invention of the equatorial astrolabe. This innovative instrument, along with its corresponding dial, enabled users to tell time with remarkable accuracy, a capability that was further illustrated through the creation of three-dimensional models.

This paper examines a decentralized device-to-device (D2D) communication network, where an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) is used to boost D2D performance. We investigate the decentralized power allocation and beamforming optimization problem to maximize D2D sum-rate under the constraints of transmit power and passive beamforming. By modeling D2D links and backhaul links as a cooperative game, we prove its supermodular nature and demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of pure Nash Equilibrium (NE). A best response algorithm is then developed to solve the power allocation and beamforming optimization problem, and its convergence to NE is shown. We further demonstrate the algorithm's ability to achieve near-optimal results through simulation results.

A novel two-dimensional Laser Doppler Vibrometry system is presented, which is an extension of the traditional point-based LDV technique. This innovative approach is utilized to examine the behavior of samples under dynamic conditions, with particular focus on films and coatings. By combining data from multiple measurement points, a comprehensive map of the sample's response can be created. This study outlines the methodology and presents findings from experiments conducted using a five-channel LDV setup, which was tested on samples subjected to acoustic excitation.

We've established that the spectra of first-order sentences with more than one variable, under binary relations, are precisely the same as the spectra of first-order sentences with unary relations, as proven by reducing the former to the latter. This discovery is based on a method that doesn't rely on specific properties of the relations, such as reflexivity or transitivity. Additionally, this result has been applied to show that the spectra of all $\mathcal{L}$-structures, where $\mathcal{L}$ contains only binary relations, can be represented as the models of a first-order sentence with unary relations.

We have developed a versatile electrostatic phase plate that can correct the Spherical Aberration in a Transmission Electron Microscope. Our approach is computationally driven and enables the creation of custom phase profiles with high precision. The use of an electron microscope's space-charge effect allows for adjustable and reconfigurable phase plates, which can be tailored to specific imaging needs. The resulting coherent and partially coherent microscope images can be optimized for specific specimen properties, leading to significant improvements in resolution and contrast. The proposed method has the potential to achieve a resolution of 0.07 Angstroms for a 100 kV microscope, and 0.05 Angstroms for a 300 kV microscope, making it a promising tool for high-resolution imaging.

In the 1940s, Feynman proposed a groundbreaking idea that quantum systems could be harnessed to simulate other quantum systems efficiently, an insight now underpinning the development of quantum computers. Over 70 years later, we have refined and expanded upon Feynman's original concept, incorporating his ideas into the formal frameworks of computational complexity and computability. Our work delves into the computational limitations of quantum circuits, examining their ability to compute functions and produce probabilistic outputs, as well as the complexity of these computations in terms of circuit depth and size. Our findings reveal a computability equivalence between a class of functions computable by quantum circuits and those calculable by Turing machines within a polynomial time frame, while also establishing a complexity equivalence between quantum circuits and a specific subclass of P. Our results provide a deeper understanding of the inherent constraints of quantum computation, particularly in simulating quantum systems, and offer new avenues for research into the computational power of quantum circuits.

The general formula for determining the possible positions after n steps of a random walk in n steps in a d-dimensional space is given by the summation formula $\sum_{i=0}^{n}\left(\begin{array}{c}n\\i\end{array}\right)d^{n-2i}$. We will present a combinatorial argument to prove this equation.

This study examines the impact of quantum field field effects on the quasinormal modes of a black hole, specifically the Schwarzschild-de Sitter (SdS) black hole. We have modified the Ricci scalar in the SdS spacetime to incorporate quantum field effects and calculated the quasinormal frequencies for the modified black hole. Our analysis reveals that quantum field effects significantly influence the quasinormal frequencies, particularly in regions close to the event horizons. We have also determined the stability of these modes and found that they are affected by quantum field effects in specific regions.

We have developed a low-energy effective model for a two-dimensional electron system in a magnetic field, based on the Dirac-Weyl equation. Our analysis reveals that the system's in-plane Hall conductivity is characterized by two massless Dirac cones, which behave similarly to charged particles with a charge of $e$. Our calculations for the system's thermal properties show that the specific heat is proportional to the square of temperature, which is consistent with previous research on similar materials. Our model also successfully explains the universal behavior of thermal transport observed in topological insulators and other unusual materials with unique electronic properties.

This research introduces ParaSpeech, a speech synthesis system capable of producing high-quality human-like speech from paragraphs of written text. To address the issue of speech discontinuity in existing full-context speech synthesis models, we developed a new approach that integrates a short-term acoustic modeling module. This ParaSpeech system utilizes the fast-GAN voice conversion system to transform short-term acoustic representations from spoken speech based on the given voice and volume levels. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms current speech synthesis models in producing coherent speech from paragraphs of text.

We introduce a new projection predictive method for making inferences about projections of high-dimensional model parameters in Bayesian variable selection. This technique excels in handling complex models with numerous variables, providing a seamless integration of variable selection and inference. By projecting high-dimensional model parameters onto a lower-dimensional space, we can efficiently perform Bayesian inference and generate reliable approximations of the posterior distribution. Our method's benefits are demonstrated through its application to various complex models, including a generalized linear model with high-dimensional coefficients, a Bayesian structural time series model, and a Bayesian change point detection model.

Recent research has highlighted the susceptibility of Deep Neural Networks to carefully crafted adversarial examples. Past studies have shown that these examples can compromise both the targeted and unintended targets due to the overfitting of adversarial training. A new technique, known as the gradient attack, enables the targeting of models that have undergone adversarial training by exploiting overfit vulnerabilities. To address this, we introduce a novel method that incorporates the detection and mitigation of adversarial examples into the training process. This method, called the Adversarial Example Filter, filters out identified adversarial examples from the training data to prevent overfitting. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the robustness of DNNs against the gradient attack and reduces the risk of model compromise through targeted attacks.

Climate change denial is often amplified by online conspiracy theories, which are increasingly prevalent on social media. To better understand the drivers of online conspiracy dissemination, we conducted a large-scale study, examining nearly 100,000 online comments from Twitter and Reddit that referenced specific conspiracy topics. Our analysis revealed that individuals who hold stronger climate change skepticism are more likely to engage with conspiracy content, particularly on Twitter. Conversely, this trend was not observed on Reddit. These findings highlight the need for targeted interventions to address climate change denial through online platforms, taking into account the unique characteristics of each site.

A search for new particles has been conducted in 13 TeV proton-proton collisions, resulting in at least two opposite-sign electrons or muons in the final state. The analysis utilized a dataset of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the CMS experiment at CERN. The study examines models of dark matter that interact with standard model particles via a scalar or pseudoscalar mediator, assuming the dark matter particles are not detectable. The presence of the mediator is inferred from the mass difference between the mediator and the dark matter particles, which is assumed to be less than the mass of the mediator. The study's findings are consistent with the predictions made for standard model interactions, leading to the exclusion of certain mediator models. For a mediator model with a 95% confidence level, the masses of mediators with couplings to standard model particles of axial-vector type are limited to 1.3 TeV for a mass difference less than the mass of the mediator, whereas mediators with couplings of a scalar type are limited to 1.0 TeV for a mass difference less than the mass of the mediator. The study also establishes the most stringent limits on the cross-section between dark matter and nucleons, which is limited to 1.1 $\times$ 10$^{-40}$ cm$^2$ for a mass difference less than the mass of the mediator, assuming that dark matter particles interact with standard model particles via a pseud

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality.

This study develops a general framework for determining unique and finite influence of various treatment options without predefined categories. Our theory is based on the use of tools that can lead to different, non-structured treatment outcomes. To achieve this, we establish a method for non-parametric analysis by establishing a set of bounds for the average treatment effect and then demonstrate how specific conditions, such as instruments affecting only one dominant factor related to treatment, can result in the unique determination of treatment effect. Our theory is further illustrated through empirical examination of the impact of diverse training programs on the earnings of young individuals in Germany.

To advance our understanding of nature's fundamental interactions, researchers are striving to create new types of antimatter particles in greater quantities. Our team has developed a novel method to produce antimatter deimerons using a combination of a positron source and a dimerized deuterium target. By utilizing a cutting-edge, high-performance positron source and a specially designed beam collimation system, we were able to achieve a breakthrough in antimatter creation. Our results show that the antideuterium particles can be produced with a significant level of efficiency, opening up exciting possibilities for new scientific discoveries.

We have developed a new numerical model to study how hierarchical triple systems gain mass, building on the work of Petrovich et al. (2019). This work examined how differential mass gain affects the orbital dynamics of these systems, causing them to experience chaotic and varying periods. We have expanded upon their findings by considering a more diverse range of initial conditions and exploring how the mass gain of the outer body components influences the dynamics. Our study reveals that when the inner component is significantly less massive than the outer component, and these components gain mass at different rates, the dynamics become particularly sensitive to the mass gain ratio. This is particularly true when the mass gain ratio is around 1.5, leading to significantly longer periods of orbital stability. We have also found that when the inner component is more massive, and these components gain mass at the same rate, the dynamics become particularly stable, with periods lasting much longer than in other scenarios.

We examine flat spacetime models that can be used to represent the universe's large-scale geometry, focusing on those with uniform expansion rates in all directions. By utilizing a specific type of coordinate system, we demonstrate that such models can be derived from a particular vacuum state, similar to the Milne universe, which can be viewed as a section of Minkowski spacetime described by de Sitter geometry in expanding coordinates. Our analysis also reveals the presence of particle effects associated with these spacetimes, the existence of a thermal bath, and the associated Hamiltonian, which can be related to the universe's large-scale entropy.

Image segmentation and image restoration tasks are typically seen as opposing processes, yet by addressing low-quality images, they share a common goal. We propose a novel approach that integrates both image segmentation and image restoration models to effectively handle complex segmentation tasks on degraded images. The introduced method, MSA-Net, combines a newly designed MSA block with existing segmentation and restoration models, demonstrating superior performance on various segmentation benchmarks using corrupted images.

Active galactic nuclei possess black holes whose mass and spin can be deduced from their observed light patterns.  A new approach to analyzing these light patterns has been developed, which involves using a specific mathematical framework to break down the observed light into distinct components.  This framework is based on the properties of a specific type of equation that describes how light travels through space, which can be used to identify the underlying physical processes shaping the observed light patterns.  This method has been successfully applied to analyzing the light patterns of supermassive black holes, which has allowed researchers to determine the mass and spin of these black holes.  This approach can be used to study the evolution of black holes over time, which can provide valuable insights into the growth and development of these celestial objects.

As interest in neuromorphic systems grows, the need for accessible tools to study and develop these systems is increasing. The PyNMF framework, an open-source emulator for neuromorphic computing, fills this need by providing a simple yet effective tool for simulating large arrays of spiking neurons and synapses. This framework is built using Python and C++ and is designed to be easy to use and modify, making it suitable for both researchers and developers. The PyNMF library includes a range of neuron models, such as leaky integrate-and-fire neurons, and allows for the simulation of complex networks of up to a million neurons and synapses. The PyNMF framework is licensed under the permissive MIT license and can be freely used and adapted.

A solar type-I noise storm is a phenomenon that is still not well understood.
We have discovered a previously unknown mechanism behind these storms, which
involves a microflare occurring in a small, moving magnetic loop. The movement
of this loop causes the plasma within it to shift, leading to electron
oscillations and the emission of radio waves. These processes are observed in
detail through simulations and the analysis of solar data. The findings show
that the radio storm's characteristics are influenced by two distinct factors:
the fluctuation of the loop's position and the change in the plasma density
due to the loop's movement. The solar simulation reveals two observable
patterns in the evolution of these factors, which are consistent with the
patterns seen in the radio emissions. The results suggest that this new model
can be used to study the movement of magnetic structures in the Sun's
atmosphere.

We have successfully captured a group of 837Rb atoms in a magneto-optical trap and taken a photograph of them for the first time using a high-sensitivity camera at a low temperature of 300 Kelvin and ambient conditions. To achieve this, we utilized a highly sensitive camera that can detect a very low rate of photons per pixel per second, combined with a bright 780 nm laser, to make the trapped atoms visible. The photograph was then analyzed to determine the trap's volume and atom distribution. The approach we developed is simple and cost-effective, making it an ideal method for visualizing a magneto-optical trap.

The impact of angular momentum on the rate at which a black hole swallows surrounding gas has been investigated.  A gas cloud rotating in the equatorial plane around a Schwarzschild black hole is considered.  By using the relativistic Euler equations, we calculated how the gas cloud collapses and accretes onto the black hole.  Our findings reveal that the mass accretion rate is significantly lower in the case of a rotating equatorial cloud compared to a non-rotating spherical cloud.  The accretion rate can be reduced by a factor of 10 or more, depending on the initial angular momentum of the cloud.  The presence of angular momentum also results in a delayed collapse of the cloud and a later onset of accretion.  The accretion rate is found to be influenced by the properties of the adiabatic equation of state, particularly the $\Gamma$-value.  The rate of mass accretion is found to be lower for higher values of $\Gamma$.

The excitation of a stationary, spherically symmetric electric dipole by a linearly polarized electromagnetic wave, as well as its interaction with a infinite plane and half-space, is investigated. The spontaneous emission rate of an excited atom nearby is also determined.

This paper investigates the proposed ground state solution for the given biharmonic Choquard type problem, for which we establish its existence. Utilizing the proposed minimization method, we are able to obtain a specific value that signifies the lowest possible value for this minimization problem.

Degraded handwritten documents often suffer from damage resulting from age,
environmental factors, or mishandling, which can severely compromise their legibility.
Restoring these documents is crucial for the preservation of historical records,
legal evidence, and artistic appreciation.
Restoring visually impaired handwritten document images is a complex task,
which requires not only enhancing their appearance but also making them more
readable.
Existing restoration techniques primarily focus on appearance enhancement,
but they may overlook the underlying structure of the text.
To address this limitation, we introduce HandWR, a new, data-driven approach for
restoring visually impaired handwritten document images.
HandWR is a two-stage process, which involves first generating a latent representation
of the underlying structure using a pre-trained model, and then integrating this
representation into an image generator to produce a fully restored image.
To improve the accuracy of the restoration, we introduce a new loss function that
takes into account the spatial relationships between handwritten characters.
To further validate the effectiveness of our approach, we create a new, large-scale
dataset consisting of 100,000 handwritten document image pairs, which are
derived from authentic historical documents.
Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our method over
existing techniques, and the ability to accurately restore complex handwritten
text, which is critical for the preservation and restoration of historical records.

This paper proposes a method to convert ID card information into a machine-readable format by converting visual data into text through image-to-text conversion technology. It involves extracting ID card images, which are then converted into text using a conversion tool. The ID card images are obtained through either manual input or automatic extraction via camera input. The process of automatically locating ID card images within an image or document is also discussed.

In vehicular communication systems, channel state information is crucial for maintaining reliable connections, which is typically obtained through pilot signals. However, due to the rapidly changing nature of vehicle channels, using only a limited number of pilot signals results in inaccurate channel tracking. To address this issue, we have developed a new approach that utilizes a combination of a sparse channel model and an optimization technique to maximize data transmission using a vehicle's available bandwidth. By minimizing the difference between the estimated and actual channel, we can improve the accuracy of channel estimation and thus increase the overall data transmission rate. The results of our simulations show that this approach can significantly enhance channel estimation accuracy and the data transmission rate, while also allowing for flexible pilot allocation.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images is a complex task that has received significant attention in the machine learning community. Developing a model that can accurately predict colors based on image content alone is a challenging task, especially when dealing with color images where the model must also account for existing colors. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called multi-task learning with image reconstruction, which involves using the existing colors in an image to generate a color map. Our experiments demonstrate that this method outperforms state-of-the-art models on multiple colorization benchmarks.

We've developed a novel numerical method for determining the weights in a class of Artificial Neural Networks, grounded in the Backpropagation algorithm and the universal approximation theorem. The resulting algorithm is equivalent to a numerical scheme of implicit time-stepping. The proof of its convergence relies on the proof of BP's correctness. The proposed method is an implicit time-stepping scheme.

A novel line interface wave phenomenon is observed at the boundary between two specially designed dual electromagnetic surfaces, and its underlying physics is mathematically explained. These surface waves can be controlled in a manner similar to semiconductors by adjusting the properties of the dual surfaces, and their speed can also be regulated. An experiment utilizing printed circuit boards demonstrated the existence of these line interface waves, and their potential applications in sub-wavelength imaging and compact component design are highlighted.

The field of cognitive robotics is characterized by its capacity to learn and adapt to dynamic environments, which often present unpredictable changes. To address this challenge, researchers have turned to multi-agent learning techniques, which enable systems to adjust to shifting environmental conditions. However, the complexity of these systems poses significant technological hurdles, particularly in terms of data collection and processing. To address this issue, we propose an advanced framework that leverages advanced data analytics to extract and interpret data from multiple sources, which can be difficult to access. This framework is composed of three key components: a data management system that organizes and integrates data from multiple sources, a multi-agent learning module that develops adaptive strategies, and a simulation platform that enables rapid testing and refinement of these strategies. By combining these components, we are able to effectively tackle the issues of data collection and processing in cognitive robotic systems, which is essential for their successful deployment in real-world settings.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been developed to enhance the reliability of statistical models that account for data variability. This estimator accounts for the variability of a data-driven model, which was initially proposed by Politis and Romano in 1993. The method has previously been utilized to create bias-corrected confidence intervals but has not been extensively applied to statistical models that consider variability, such as the median regression model. This study adapts the bias-corrected estimator to establish confidence intervals for the regression parameters in the median regression model. The proposed estimator outperforms an existing method, particularly in scenarios involving smaller sample sizes. A simulation experiment demonstrates the practical application and effectiveness of the bias-corrected estimator when applied to statistical models that account for data variability.

The task of identifying and categorizing relationships between entities within text is a fundamental aspect of a natural language understanding system. This paper presents an innovative method for this purpose, leveraging pre-trained language models and a novel technique called label-free learning. By utilizing pre-trained language models, the proposed method captures the inherent meaning of words and their contextual relationships, enabling more accurate and robust relationship extraction. The label-free learning approach involves training the model using a dataset that contains only entity mentions, without any mention of the relationships between them. This method has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets, including a recently introduced dataset with a more challenging set of labels. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing methods that rely on supervised learning, particularly in scenarios where the training data is limited. The method's ability to learn from data that is more representative of real-world scenarios also makes it a promising approach for improving the robustness of relationship extraction systems.

The impact of anisotropy on the dissociation of quarkonia in multi-dimensional space is investigated.  Our analysis reveals that the $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ states exhibit similar dissociation behaviors in 5-dimensional space, with both reaching a dissociation point at approximately 200 MeV.  However, the separation between these quarkonia becomes more pronounced at higher temperatures in 4-dimensional space.  Our findings also indicate that the anisotropy factor that causes a 50% drop in the yield of the excited $\psi(2S)$ state is lower than that of the $J/\psi$ state.  Our results further show that the anisotropy factor that causes a 50% drop in the yield of the $J/\psi$ state is lower in 5-dimensional space than that of the $\psi(2S)$ state, with the opposite being true for the $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$ states.

The magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7 have been thoroughly investigated through a combination of experimental and theoretical methods, including neutron diffraction, muon-spin rotation, and ab-initio calculations. Our research reveals that the material exhibits canted ferromagnetic behavior on both Ru1 and Ru2 sites with an internal magnetic field of 0.16 mu0 and 0.14 mu0 respectively, when observed at 15 K. Interestingly, this field increases as the temperature decreases, ultimately leading to a complete collapse of the magnetic structure below 4 K. Our study also indicates that the muon sites in Tb3RuO7 are free from significant electric field gradients, and that the material undergoes a series of spin reorientation transitions at 12 K, 9 K, and 6 K. Our ab-initio calculations suggest that these transitions are driven by the interplay between the magnetic and lattice properties of Tb3RuO7.

Machine learning models for processing signals, such as images and audio, have been widely used, but their direct application to video processing is not feasible due to the massive size of raw data. A new type of model architecture, called an image or audio MLP, has been developed to overcome this limitation. These models use a small set of learned embeddings to represent entire images or audio clips, which can then be processed efficiently. However, this concept has not been successfully applied to videos until now. In this paper, we introduce an innovative MLP model that combines two separate layers of processing to represent both the spatial and temporal components of a video. This new architecture allows us to effectively represent videos at a much lower data size, which in turn enables the efficient processing of large video datasets. As a result, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on various video processing tasks, including classification, retrieval, and prediction, while also offering significant data compression benefits.

We introduce a novel, unsupervised method for improving semi-supervised learning through covariate shift adaptation. Our approach leverages both labeled and unlabeled data from the target domain to correct the bias introduced by distribution changes. This method is further enhanced by incorporating semi-supervised learning techniques, which we demonstrate can be effectively applied to the adjusted target domain. As a result, our method achieves superior performance compared to existing supervised and semi-supervised adaptation techniques, particularly in scenarios where there is a significant distribution shift between the source and target domains.

Recent research has demonstrated that the performance of deep learning models is influenced by their geometric properties. To further investigate this, we analyze the geometric architecture of three types of deep learning systems: convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and transformers. We then examine the geometric properties of these models in relation to their performance, specifically in terms of classification accuracy and generalization error.

We provide a detailed explanation for the existence of specific generators in the reduced part of the narrow class group of real quadratic fields, based on the properties of minimal solutions to Pell's equation. As a consequence, we establish the infeasibility of certain hypotheses regarding real composite quadratic fields, particularly those with a prime factorization containing a large number of distinct primes.

A new, advanced technique for identifying specific particle formations within complex jet signals has been developed and implemented within the ATLAS experiment's software framework. This method leverages a combination of specialized variables and deep neural networks to achieve superior accuracy. Our study showcases the effectiveness of this technique in two distinct particle formation tags, namely, W boson ghost and top quark tags, and also highlights its potential as a versatile tool for other particle tags that are more susceptible to background interference.

We introduce a modified version of associated Stirling numbers, which consider the minimum size of subsets containing single-element sets marked with an 'r'. The r-associated Stirling numbers of the second kind count specific partitions of a set with marked elements, while the r-associated Stirling numbers of the first kind count permutations with specific properties.

This study presents a computational approach for deriving layer group characteristics, utilizing the GAP system. We have developed specific packages to compute key properties of these groups, such as their conjugacy classes and projective representations, in three-dimensional space. By leveraging a computer, we can efficiently calculate these characteristics and generate their corresponding GAP representations. Furthermore, we have incorporated a method for calculating the symmetry properties of tensor components under layer group transformations, allowing us to derive a formula for determining invariant tensor components. To demonstrate the practical application of our method, we have applied it to a crystal structure, successfully identifying all invariant tensor components.

Momentum operators are examined in the context of intrinsically curved spaces, specifically focusing on real, compact spaces with a positive curvature, which necessitates a discrete topology. This investigation is carried out within the framework of spectral geometry, where the geometry of a Riemann surface is defined through its associated Laplace operator, represented as a Jordan triangle in terms of its spectrum. By employing a Jordan triangle representation, momentum operators can be introduced, enabling the definition of geodesic spaces and curved planes, generalizing the concept of flat planes.

Using the worldline formulation, we've developed a method to overcome the sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations by mapping it to a phase problem that can be addressed through a novel approach. This new method involves reformulating the issue in terms of a filling-dependent variable, which allows us to develop a filling schedule that ensures zero average phase fluctuations at each point. This solution is particularly effective for systems with short-range interactions, and we've demonstrated its utility through simulations of the 2D Hubbard model, where we found that the sign problem can be completely eliminated for intermediate fillings, and partially addressed for others.

Our proposed composite Higgs model is based on a global $U(2)$ symmetry, which is broken down to $Sp(2)$ by four composite Higgs fields. These Higgs fields are represented as a $2\times 2$ Hermitian matrix composed of a complex and a real scalar. The complex scalar is responsible for acquiring a non-zero vacuum expectation value, while the real scalar does not. This setup results in the Higgs sector being described by a linear sigma model featuring a potential with a "bump" at the origin. We find that this "bump" can be the target of new physics, leading to observable signatures in the Higgs sector.

Our virtual reality system incorporates Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations to enhance user immersion by synchronizing real-world and virtual experiences. This paper outlines our approach and evaluates VR applications with VPPMs in two studies. The first study examines the user feedback on a range of VPPMs, including their effects on vision, hearing, and physical interactions in both physical and virtual environments. The second study compares VR experiences with and without VPPMs, using a test involving users' ability to locate hidden objects in a 360-degree video. The results indicate that VR users generally respond positively to VPPMs, and their use improves object recognition and user immersion.

We investigate the feasibility of adding new programming languages to CodeBERT, a pre-trained code representation model, without retraining the entire model. Our study focuses on two languages, Julia and Swift, and we explore various techniques, including fine-tuning CodeBERT on instruction-following datasets, using a two-stage process with masked language modeling followed by task-specific training, and utilizing a separate classifier for masked language modeling. Our results indicate that fine-tuning CodeBERT on instruction-following datasets yields the best performance, with a 20.4% increase in accuracy for Julia and a 10.9% increase for Swift compared to baseline models.
